lead: On the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus the readings of Year B lead us from the heart of God in the Old Testament to the pierced heart of Christ on the Cross. In Hosea, God speaks as a father who taught his little son to walk and cannot bear to give him up: “My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.” St Paul kneels before the Father and prays that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. In the Gospel a soldier pierces the side of the dead Jesus, and blood and water flow out.

The response is the song of Isaiah 12: “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.” Pope Pius XII took the first words of this verse in Latin, Haurietis aquas, as the title of his letter on devotion to the Sacred Heart (1956). The solemnity is kept on the Friday after the Second Sunday after Pentecost, which this year falls on 4 June.

r.h: How can I give you up?
set: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ, in the years before it fell to Assyria in 722. His own painful marriage became a parable of God’s love for an unfaithful people (chapters 1–3). Chapter 11 turns from the image of husband and wife to that of father and child.

The Lectionary leaves out the verses of judgment (vv. 2, 5–8b): Israel ran after the Baals, refused to return, and would go into exile. Our verses keep the two ends of the poem: the tender love of the beginning and God’s refusal to destroy at the end.
str: v. 1: Israel as a child: “out of Egypt I called my son”.
vv. 3–4: God the parent: teaching to walk, carrying, healing, leading with cords of kindness, bending down to feed.
v. 8c: the turning point: God’s own heart recoils.
v. 9: “I am God and no mortal, the Holy One in your midst.”
kw: In Hebrew the heart is not only feelings but the centre of thought, decision and love. When God says “my heart”, he speaks of his innermost self.
From the same root as the “overthrow” of Sodom and Gomorrah. Instead of overthrowing Israel like the cities of the plain, God’s own heart is turned over within him.
God’s holiness is his being utterly other. Here it is surprising: precisely because he is God and not a man, he does not act in anger. His holiness shows itself as mercy.
vv: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.
The Exodus was an act of fatherly love. St Matthew sees this verse fulfilled when the child Jesus returns from Egypt (Matthew 2:15): the true Son relives the story of Israel.
Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, I took them up in my arms;
Ephraim is a name for the northern kingdom. God pictures himself holding the hands of a toddler. Few passages in the Old Testament are so tender.
I led them with cords of human kindness, with bands of love.

Not the ropes used to drive animals, but the bonds of love that draw a child. Textual note: in the next line the Hebrew words for “infant” and “yoke” are written with the same consonants, so some translations read “like those who lift infants to their cheeks” and others “like those who ease the yoke on their jaws”. Both pictures speak of tender care.
My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.
Admah and Zeboiim, named just before, were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). God’s justice would allow it, but his heart will not.
for I am God and no mortal, the Holy One in your midst,
A human father might give up a rebellious son. God does not. His love is more faithful than any human love.
ch: The Church reads Hosea on this day because the heart of God, revealed to the prophets, has taken flesh in Jesus. Pope Pius XII taught in Haurietis Aquas that the Old Testament already speaks of God’s love in such tender human terms, and that these images prepare for the human heart of the Word made flesh (in substance). God’s covenant love for Israel is not withdrawn (Romans 11:29). The Catechism teaches that Jesus has loved us all with a human heart (CCC 478).

r.h: The love of Christ that surpasses knowledge
set: The Letter to the Ephesians presents itself as written by Paul in prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul after his death, in his name and spirit; others defend Paul’s own authorship. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Its great theme is the mystery of God’s plan: to unite all things in Christ, and to bring Jews and Gentiles together into one body, the Church.
Our passage has two parts. First Paul speaks of the grace given to him, the least of all the saints, to preach the riches of Christ to the Gentiles. Then he kneels and prays for his readers.
str: vv. 8–9: the grace given to Paul: to preach the boundless riches of Christ and to make known the hidden plan.
vv. 10–12: through the Church God’s wisdom is made known even to the heavenly powers; in Christ we have access to God.
vv. 14–15: Paul kneels before the Father, from whom every family takes its name.
vv. 16–19: his prayer: strength in the inner being, Christ dwelling in the heart, the knowledge of a love beyond knowledge, the fullness of God.
kw: Literally “that cannot be tracked”, whose footprints cannot be traced to the end. The riches of Christ are beyond exploring.
A play on words: patēr, father, and patria, family or clan. Every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from the Father.
The goal of the prayer is that we be filled with all the fullness of God: not a little of God, but God himself living in us.
vv: this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ,
Paul, who once persecuted the Church, calls himself the very least of the saints. Grace, not his merit, made him an apostle.
in whom we have access to God in boldness and confidence through faith in him.
Through Christ we may approach God not as frightened strangers but as children who speak openly to their Father.
For this reason I bow my knees before the Father,
Jews usually prayed standing. Kneeling shows special humility and urgency.
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.
Two images: a plant rooted in soil and a house built on a foundation. Love is both the soil and the foundation.
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge,
A deliberate paradox: we are to know what is beyond knowing. This knowledge is not information but experience, the knowledge of the heart.
ch: The Church has seen in “the breadth and length and height and depth” the dimensions of the Cross, on which Christ’s love stretched out to the whole world; St Augustine read the verse in this way (in substance). Pope Francis, in his letter on the love of the heart of Christ, Dilexit Nos (2024), invited the Church to rediscover this love that surpasses knowledge, and to let it reach the wounded heart of the world.

r.h: Blood and water from his side
set: Jesus has just died on the cross with the words “It is finished” (19:30). It is Friday afternoon, the day of Preparation, and that evening a solemn sabbath begins; in John’s Gospel it is also the eve of the Passover. The Law said that a hanged body must not remain overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). So the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified men broken, which hastened death, and the bodies taken down.

Background. When John speaks of “the Jews” in this passage, he means the religious authorities who were dealing with Pilate, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his mother, the disciples and the evangelist were themselves Jews. The Church firmly teaches that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: v. 31: the request to break the legs and remove the bodies before the sabbath.
vv. 32–33: the soldiers break the legs of the two others, but Jesus is already dead.
v. 34: a soldier pierces his side; blood and water come out.
v. 35: the eyewitness testifies so that you may believe.
vv. 36–37: two Scriptures fulfilled: “None of his bones shall be broken”; “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
kw: The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the rib taken from Adam’s side to form Eve (Genesis 2:21–22). The Fathers saw the Church, the new Eve, formed from the side of the new Adam.

The Greek word means to prick or pierce. St Augustine, reading the Latin “opened”, said that a door of life was opened there, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed (in substance, Tractates on John 120).
The eyewitness, understood by the Church as the beloved disciple, stresses that he saw this. It is not a legend but a witness given so that we may believe.
vv: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.
Jesus has given up his spirit willingly. His death is real and complete.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
Blood and water: the sign of a real human death, and, for the evangelist, a sign of the life that flows from it. Jesus had promised rivers of living water from his heart (7:37–39).
His testimony is true, and he knows that he tells the truth.
The evangelist turns directly to the reader: “so that you also may believe”. This scene is at the heart of John’s witness.
None of his bones shall be broken.
The rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), and also the psalm of the righteous one whom God protects (Psalm 34:20). Jesus is the true Passover Lamb.
They will look on the one whom they have pierced.
From Zechariah 12:10, where the people mourn over one they pierced, and a spirit of compassion is poured out. To look on the Pierced One is to begin to be converted.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the blood and water that flowed from the pierced side of the crucified Jesus are types of Baptism and the Eucharist, the sacraments of new life (CCC 1225), and that the Church was born from the pierced heart of Christ, as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam (CCC 766, quoting St Ambrose in substance). St John Chrysostom told the newly baptised that the water and the blood are symbols of Baptism and the Eucharist, and that from these the Church is born (in substance, Catecheses 3).

Devotion to the Sacred Heart is not devotion to an organ apart from the person. The heart of Jesus is the sign of the whole love of the Son of God, divine and human, for the Father and for us. The Catechism says that the Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the chief sign and symbol of that love with which the divine Redeemer continually loves the eternal Father and all human beings without exception (CCC 478, in substance).

qa: Why do we honour the heart of Jesus? Is it not enough to love Jesus himself?

We do honour Jesus himself. The heart is the biblical sign of the person’s innermost self and love. To honour the Sacred Heart is to worship the person of the Word made flesh, under the sign of his human heart, pierced for us. Because his human heart belongs to the divine person of the Son, the Church honours it with the worship given to Christ himself (compare CCC 478).
What are the promises connected with the Sacred Heart, such as the nine first Fridays?

They come from the private revelations given to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial in France between 1673 and 1675. The Church approved the devotion and recommends the practice of receiving Communion on the first Friday of the month in reparation and love. Private revelations do not add to the faith (CCC 67); the heart of the devotion is the love of Christ shown on the Cross and in the Eucharist, and our response of love and reparation.
Does Hosea’s tenderness mean that God does not judge sin?

No. The chapter itself speaks of exile as the result of Israel’s refusal to return (vv. 5–7). But judgment is not God’s last word. His mercy is greater than his anger, and he punishes in order to heal and bring back. On the Cross the justice and the mercy of God meet: the Son bears the sin of the world, and the heart pierced by sin pours out forgiveness.
rite: Devotion to the heart of Jesus grew in the Middle Ages among saints such as St Bernard, St Gertrude and St Mechtilde. St John Eudes composed the first liturgical texts for the feast in the seventeenth century, and after the revelations to St Margaret Mary Alacoque, with the support of St Claude de la Colombière, the devotion spread throughout the Church. Blessed Pius IX extended the feast to the whole Latin Church in 1856, and Pope Leo XIII consecrated the human race to the Sacred Heart in 1899. In many Catholic homes in India a picture of the Sacred Heart has a place of honour, with a lamp burning before it, and families renew the enthronement of the Sacred Heart in the home. This day is also kept as a day of prayer for the holiness of priests, as Pope St John Paul II asked.
study: Hosea pictures God teaching a child to walk. When have I felt God carrying me or bending down to me?
Paul prays that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith. What would need to change in my heart for him to be at home there?
The evangelist says, “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.” How can I look at a crucifix today with new eyes?
How can our family honour the Sacred Heart in our home, in prayer, and in reparation for the wounds of the world?
